column4: The noble, swift horses, الصَّافِنَاتُ الْجِيَادُ, are the Quran's explicit presentation of the animal inferred in 100:1 from breath, stride, and speed.
Solomon's حُبَّ الْخَيْرِ joins love of valuable horses to ذِكْرِ رَبِّي; the section explicitly sets this beside the human's love of khayr and ingratitude to his Lord.
رُدُّوهَا عَلَيَّ returns the horses of 38:31-32, and touching their legs and necks makes their trained body—the section's legs, narrowed frame, and service to an owner—visible.
الْخَيْلِ الْمُسَوَّمَةِ places horses inside the decorated human love of desires and stored wealth, directly supporting the section's two faces of the horse as runner and loved property.
Horses are made لِتَرْكَبُوهَا وَزِينَةً, coupling the rider-facing body developed from insiyy with the horse as an object of adornment and desire.
كُلِّ ضَامِرٍ is a lean mount arriving from a distant pass; it concretizes the source dictionary's damura, the trained horse pared down until it resembles an arrow shaft.
رِبَاطِ الْخَيْلِ presents horses held ready as concentrated power for a collective purpose, matching the trained animal that gathers its whole run for its owner's work.
Ships and cattle are made as مَا تَرْكَبُونَ; the mount-human relation supplies the concrete setting for the source dictionary's animal side nearest the rider.
The rider settles on the mount's back and must remember the Lord's favor, turning the section's horse-and-owner relation into a demand that the human acknowledge his own Lord.
وَإِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ places return to the Lord in the rider's mouth, answering the section's human who is attached to property yet will be exposed before his Lord.
Immediately after the mount and remembrance scene, إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَكَفُورٌ states the same human ingratitude that follows the running animal in surah 100.
Humans are made owners of livestock created by God, فَهُمْ لَهَا مَالِكُونَ, establishing the lower owner-animal relation against which the section measures the human-Lord relation.
وَذَلَّلْنَاهَا لَهُمْ and فَمِنْهَا رَكُوبُهُمْ show the animal's body subjected for human riding, the same bodily service the section hears in breath and sees in legs.
After the animals' benefits, أَفَلَا يَشْكُرُونَ exposes the missing gratitude; it is the exact moral turn made when the devoted horse is followed by the kanud human.
وَالصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا is the section's stated parallel: an oath introduces a feminine plural known by its action rather than a supplied name.
فَالزَّاجِرَاتِ زَجْرًا adds the next action with fa, directly paralleling the running, striking, raising, and entering stages chained in surah 100.
فَالتَّالِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا completes the action-defined oath sequence begun in 37:1; its own contribution is the third immediately linked act.
وَالْمُرْسَلَاتِ عُرْفًا is the section's second stated parallel, an oath by a feminine plural identified through what it does.
فَالْعَاصِفَاتِ عَصْفًا makes a following burst of force with fa, directly corresponding to the section's uninterrupted acceleration from one act to the next.
وَالنَّاشِرَاتِ نَشْرًا continues the same unnamed collective through another staged action; it extends the sequence named by 77:1-2.
فَالْفَارِقَاتِ فَرْقًا supplies a further fa-linked act, showing how an oath can define agents cumulatively through successive effects.
فَالْمُلْقِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا completes the continuing chain with what the agents deliver, as each surah-100 participle adds a new consequence of motion.
وَالذَّارِيَاتِ ذَرْوًا opens another oath with an unnamed feminine plural discerned by an energetic action.
فَالْحَامِلَاتِ وِقْرًا turns immediately by fa from scattering to bearing, closely matching the section's reading of chained stages as one developing movement.
فَالْجَارِيَاتِ يُسْرًا contributes literal running or coursing inside the action-defined oath chain, a direct counterpart to the runners of 100:1.
فَالْمُقَسِّمَاتِ أَمْرًا gives the chain's next assigned act, reinforcing how the subjects are disclosed by their ordered work.
وَالنَّازِعَاتِ غَرْقًا begins an oath series of feminine plurals whose identities are carried by strenuous acts, like the horse disclosed by exertion.
وَالنَّاشِطَاتِ نَشْطًا adds another bodily force to the unnamed group sequence and prepares the transition into rapid movement.
وَالسَّابِحَاتِ سَبْحًا makes flowing motion itself the group's designation, parallel to recognizing the animal solely from its gait.
فَالسَّابِقَاتِ سَبْقًا joins fa-linked acceleration to overtaking; the source dictionary likewise calls the horse's run a witness to its sabq.
فَالْمُدَبِّرَاتِ أَمْرًا completes the movement with purposeful execution, matching the section's emphasis that accumulated speed is given to a task.
وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ makes dawn breathe inside an oath; it strikingly joins the section's audible breath to the morning reached by the running sequence.
وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا directly restates the intense human love of property that the section hears in لِحُبِّ الْخَيْرِ لَشَدِيدٌ.
جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ redirects gathering from the source dictionary's horse collecting its run into one thrust to a human collecting and counting wealth.
بَلِ الْإِنسَانُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ بَصِيرَةٌ is the clearest nonlexical parallel to the human being evidence against himself in 100:7.
وَشَهِدُوا عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ makes the human beings' own testimony establish their unbelief, matching the section's reading of testimony against one's own ingratitude.
شَهِدُوا عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا كَافِرِينَ gives the same self-incriminating witness that contrasts with the horse's run witnessing in its favor.
شَاهِدِينَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ بِالْكُفْرِ sets testimony explicitly against the witnesses themselves, the human side of the section's horse-human reversal.
Tongues, hands, and feet تَشْهَدُ عَلَيْهِمْ with what they did; a body's own action becomes evidence, as the horse's running body proves its quality and the human body indicts its owner.
Hands speak and feet تَشْهَدُ بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ, making the very limbs that carried human action bear adverse witness.
Hearing, sight, and skins شَهِدَ عَلَيْهِمْ, sharply developing the section's contrast between a horse's bodily performance testifying for it and the human body testifying against him.
The condemned ask their skins لِمَ شَهِدتُّمْ عَلَيْنَا; this row contributes the explicit recognition that one's own body has become an adverse witness.
In a battle setting, God tests what is in the breasts and purifies what is in the hearts; this directly answers the section's human chest whose contents will be sorted after the charge.
أَلَا حِينَ يَثْنُونَ صُدُورَهُمْ describes an attempted inward concealment and says God knows what is hidden, clarifying why the human chest cannot remain closed.
يَعْلَمُ ... وَمَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ states that what breasts hide is already known, corresponding directly to the later extraction of their contents.
يَوْمَ تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ states without the chest word that inward secrets will be tested, the same disclosure staged in the section's final horse-human contrast.
This ayah joins kufr versus gratitude, return to your Lord, and إِنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ; it gathers the section's human ingratitude and exposed chest into one statement.
يَوْمَئِذٍ يَصْدُرُ النَّاسُ أَشْتَاتًا uses the named ṣ-d-r root for people issuing forth at judgment, while the source dictionary uses it for a horse arriving first by its chest.
سَيُهْزَمُ الْجَمْعُ gives the battlefield fate of a gathered force, the same kind of jamʿ into whose middle the surah-100 runners plunge.
After a catalogue of powers placed in human service, إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَظَلُومٌ كَفَّارٌ makes the same turn from devoted provision to the ungrateful human.
The Lord makes ships run for humans so that they seek His bounty; this vehicle's commanded service supplies a close non-animal parallel to the mount spent in its owner's work.
After the carrying vessel has saved them, the humans turn away and وَكَانَ الْإِنسَانُ كَفُورًا; the service-to-ingratitude sequence directly matches the section.
Fire is produced from a green tree, فَإِذَا أَنتُم مِّنْهُ تُوقِدُونَ; like sparks struck from the runner's contact with stone, an apparently contrary material releases fire.
فَمَا أَوْجَفْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ خَيْلٍ makes the absence of spurred horses legally decisive; it is a precise boundary around the fastest horse-run that animates the section.
Believers are أَشَدُّ حُبًّا لِّلَّهِ, reversing the human who is shadid in love of property by directing the same intensity toward God.
The ayah sets possessions, profitable trade, and pleasing homes against love of God, His Messenger, and striving, defining the loyalty at stake in the section's love-of-khayr comparison.
لَا تُلْهِيهِمْ تِجَارَةٌ وَلَا بَيْعٌ عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ supplies the faithful side of the ambiguity in Solomon's love of horses in relation to remembrance of his Lord.
لَا تُلْهِكُمْ أَمْوَالُكُمْ ... عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ gives the explicit boundary between loved property and remembrance that the section opens through 38:32.
لَن تَنَالُوا الْبِرَّ حَتَّىٰ تُنفِقُوا مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ turns attachment to valued property into its relinquishment for righteousness.
وَلَا تَعْدُ عَيْنَاكَ عَنْهُمْ uses the source's ʿ-d-w root for the eyes passing beyond people toward زِينَةَ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا, redirecting the runner-root away from worldly adornment.
أَشَدَّ النَّاسِ عَدَاوَةً brings together sh-d-d and ʿ-d-w—the two source roots glossed as the horse's run—but in the human sense of most intense enmity.
يَعْدُونَ فِي السَّبْتِ uses ʿ-d-w for crossing the Lord's limit; the root that names the animal's fastest run becomes human transgression.
Moses is told اضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ الْحَجَرَ and water bursts from stone; striking stone releases water here, rather than the runner's fire-spark.
أَنِ اضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ الْحَجَرَ again makes a struck stone yield springs, a concrete elemental reversal of hooves striking sparks.
إِنَّ أَنكَرَ الْأَصْوَاتِ لَصَوْتُ الْحَمِيرِ names an animal's own cry, sharpening the section's express boundary: ḍabḥ is exerted breath, neither neigh nor other call.
The ayah says blindness belongs to الْقُلُوبُ الَّتِي فِي الصُّدُورِ; where the horse's chest visibly wins, the human chest houses an unseen moral failure.
فَاسْتَبِقُوا الْخَيْرَاتِ redirects the source dictionary's sabq, proof of a horse's excellence, into human competition for good deeds.
فَاسْتَبِقُوا الْخَيْرَاتِ again turns speed and precedence toward good, opposing the human whose intense drive terminates in loved wealth.
يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ وَهُمْ لَهَا سَابِقُونَ combines haste and precedence in good works, the ethical counterpart of the horse's excellent, outstripping run.
سَابِقُوا إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ commands humans to race toward forgiveness, redirecting the section's bodily race toward the proper human goal.
وَالسَّابِقُونَ السَّابِقُونَ transfers distinction through precedence from the well-bred racer to the foremost human beings before God.
Livestock carry burdens to a land people could reach only with severe bodily effort; beside the horses of 16:8, it makes an animal's expenditure of body for its owner explicit.
Cattle provide drink, many benefits, and food; this repeated animal-to-human service enlarges the contrast with the human who withholds gratitude from his own provider.
وَعَلَيْهَا وَعَلَى الْفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ places the human physically upon the carrying animal, corresponding to the source dictionary's rider-facing side.
God makes cattle so that some are ridden and some eaten, another direct instance of an animal body fitted to human use.
Humans obtain needs through livestock and are carried on them and ships; the ayah develops the total service that the section attributes to the trained horse.
Sacrificial camels are سَخَّرْنَاهَا لَكُمْ and humans are told to mention God over them, joining a subjected animal body to acknowledgement of its true giver.
Neither flesh nor blood reaches God, but human taqwa does; this distinguishes the animal's offered body from the inward human quality sought by the Lord.
God subjects ships to run by His command for human benefit, beginning the service catalogue that culminates in the ungrateful human of 14:34.
The sun and moon are دَائِبَيْنِ, ceaselessly performing their appointed motion for humans; their sustained service adds a cosmic analogue to the horse's total exertion.
أَمْ نَحْنُ جَمِيعٌ مُّنتَصِرٌ voices a gathered host's confidence; 54:45 then supplies that jamʿ's defeat, paralleling the force entered in 100:5.
يَوْمَ الْتَقَى الْجَمْعَانِ names the battlefield meeting of two gathered forces, giving concrete military context to the jamʿ reached by the charge.
يَوْمَ الْتَقَى الْجَمْعَانِ again locates jamʿ in an actual battle encounter, rather than only in the source dictionary's secondary sense of gathering the horse's run.
وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَى depicts a human gathering and hoarding, another pointed redirection of the horse's collected motion into possessiveness.
أَلَّن نَّجْمَعَ عِظَامَهُ moves jamʿ from the horse collecting its living run to God's reassembling the human body for judgment.
إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا uses khayr for property left at death, confirming the wealth sense that underlies the human's حُبِّ الْخَيْرِ in the section.
وَأَجْلِبْ عَلَيْهِم بِخَيْلِكَ وَرَجِلِكَ stages cavalry and infantry brought against people; it is the Quran's other compact scene of horse-borne assault amid a force.
أَفَرَأَيْتُمُ النَّارَ الَّتِي تُورُونَ uses the same ignition verb heard in 100:2, moving from hoof-made sparks to the fire humans kindle.
آنَسْتُ نَارًا uses the named hamza-nun-sin root in the different sense of perceiving fire; it meets both the source's rider-facing insiyy and the charge's sparks without replacing either sense.
إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا repeats the hamza-nun-sin/fire conjunction and adds a sought burning brand, a specific secondary meeting of the section's insan-root and ignition image.
آنَسَ مِن جَانِبِ الطُّورِ نَارًا again uses the named root for perceiving fire on a journey; the explicit side, journey, and fire make the secondary echo especially concrete.
كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًا makes the person sufficient evidence for his own reckoning, a non-witness-root parallel to self-testimony in the section.
The sinners could not hide from their own hearing, sight, and skins testifying; the ayah explains the failed concealment implied by the bodily witnesses in 41:20-21.
Every soul arrives مَعَهَا سَائِقٌ وَشَهِيدٌ; driver and witness surround the judged human, echoing the section's rider relation and its transformed witness language.
The earth تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا, so a nonhuman thing reports what occurred through it; this parallels bodily action serving as its own evidence.
وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَيَعْلَمُ مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ states the Lord's knowledge of what breasts conceal, the hidden content later brought out in the section.
وَرَبُّكَ يَعْلَمُ مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ repeats the conceal/reveal pair under the Lord's knowledge, strengthening the chest's role as temporary enclosure rather than refuge.

أَوَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِأَعْلَمَ بِمَا فِي صُدُورِ الْعَالَمِينَ challenges a public claim of faith by the inward content God knows, matching the section's move from outward human stance to inner evidence.
Return to God, disclosure of deeds, and عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ connect the chest's hidden contents to the final accounting that follows the horse scene.
إِنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ places the breast's contents within God's wider knowledge of every hidden thing.
After truth is established and falsehood erased, إِنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ makes the inward content part of what cannot survive concealed or falsified.
God knows what humans hide and reveal and is عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ, directly corresponding to the section's sorting of what lies within chests.
Whether speech is concealed or voiced, إِنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ; inwardness does not shield the human from the Lord's knowledge.
عَدُوِّي وَعَدُوَّكُمْ uses the runner-root in the human enemy sense while warning against offering affection to enemies of the Lord, joining the section's root echo to misdirected attachment.
Some spouses and children are عَدُوًّا لَّكُمْ; the runner-root's enemy sense appears inside the very attachments that can compete with loyalty to the Lord.
إِنَّمَا أَمْوَالُكُمْ وَأَوْلَادُكُمْ فِتْنَةٌ identifies possessions and family as a test, clarifying why intense love of khayr is morally diagnostic.
قُتِلَ الْإِنسَانُ مَا أَكْفَرَهُ gives the same stark judgment of the human's ingratitude toward his maker, though without the horse comparison.
After God gives life, death, and life again, إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَكَفُورٌ ties human ingratitude to the Lord who controls his whole course and return.
إِنَّا ذَهَبْنَا نَسْتَبِقُ is a literal human race; it plausibly makes physical the horse-human transfer of sabq, but its narrative purpose is the brothers' alibi rather than moral striving.
لَا الشَّمْسُ يَنبَغِي لَهَا أَن تُدْرِكَ الْقَمَرَ sets a boundary on overtaking within ordered motion; it only indirectly illuminates the racehorse whose excellence is proved by overtaking.
فَلَا أُقْسِمُ بِالْخُنَّسِ opens an oath by entities identified through retreating motion, another close instance of the section's unnamed oath-subjects disclosed by what they do.
الْجَوَارِ الْكُنَّسِ identifies the oath-subjects as coursing and disappearing; their running both echoes the 100:1 runners and meets the horses hidden behind the veil in 38:32.
أَلْهَاكُمُ التَّكَاثُرُ makes acquisitive increase distract the human, a direct development of the section's intense attachment to property.
حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ carries distraction by increase straight to the graves, the same abrupt passage from love of wealth to opened graves in surah 100.
The wealth-gatherer thinks أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ; this ayah contributes the delusion attached to the gathering named in 104:2.
نَارُ اللَّهِ الْمُوقَدَةُ joins the wealth-gatherer's fate to kindled fire, a specific meeting of the section's property attachment and its ignition image.
الَّتِي تَطَّلِعُ عَلَى الْأَفْئِدَةِ carries that fire into human hearts, joining the wealth scene to the section's eventual exposure of what lies inside the chest.
كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ بِالْقِسْطِ شُهَدَاءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِكُمْ commands precisely the self-opposing witness that the section reads in the human's testimony against himself.
وَلَوْ أَلْقَىٰ مَعَاذِيرَهُ says excuses cannot displace the self-knowledge stated in 75:14, clarifying the force of the human's adverse testimony.
Whether people hide what is in their breasts or disclose it, God knows it; this directly parallels the section's chest as a temporary container whose contents will be brought out.
The remembered covenant and وَقُلْتُمْ سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا are followed by God's knowledge of breasts, joining pledged service to the inward reality that will test it.
Within a battle encounter, the enemy is shown as few and God is عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ; the gathered-force setting and inward knowledge meet two distinct details of the section.
وَآتَى الْمَالَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ makes loved wealth something the righteous give, rather than the terminus of the human's intense attachment.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way enact the section's misdirected love of property and prepare the bodily fire scene in 9:35.

Hoarded wealth is heated in hellfire and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs; the ayah specifically joins property, fire, and the body, images the section holds together around the horse-human comparison.

نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ إِنَّهُ أَوَّابٌ establishes Solomon as an excellent, returning servant before the horses appear, materially informing the two possible relations between horse-love and remembrance of his Lord.
Immediately after decorated desires including horses, the ayah asks whether it should announce what is better and locates the enduring reward عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ.
الْمَالُ وَالْبَنُونَ زِينَةُ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا names property as worldly adornment, then prefers enduring righteous deeds; it supplies the boundary for the decorated horses and wealth of 3:14.
Worldly life is adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth before it withers; this reverses the apparent durability promised by intense love of valuable property.
فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَذَرُوا الْبَيْعَ commands movement toward remembrance and away from trade, a direct ethical reorientation of both running and property-love.
When people see trade or amusement they disperse toward it and leave the messenger standing; bodily movement toward gain realizes the danger opened by Solomon's horse-love in relation to remembrance.
The breast opened to submission is opposed to a breast made constricted and tight; the human chest carries guidance or refusal, unlike the horse's chest whose exertion is outwardly evident.
A breast opened to submission and light from its Lord is set against hardened hearts, specifying the inward human condition hidden within the ṣadr.
The sky أَذِنَتْ لِرَبِّهَا وَحُقَّتْ listens to its Lord as it undergoes its assigned act, the creation-level counterpart to the horse giving itself to an owner and the human failing his Lord.
The earth likewise listens to its Lord and is bound to do so, repeating the obedience that throws the section's human ingratitude into relief.
The lamp's oil nearly gives light وَلَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نَارٌ; fire almost appearing without contact forms a precise boundary against the runner's contact-made sparks.
وَمَا يُغْنِي عَنْهُ مَالُهُ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ states that wealth cannot serve its owner at his fall, opposing the animal body that does serve its owner with the property the human trusts.
The ayah contrasts the believers' love with concealed hatred and closes with God's knowledge of breasts, making the chest the place where an outward relationship's contrary truth resides.
وَهُوَ عَلِيمٌ بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ repeats the direct formulation that the contents of human breasts are already known before their final extraction.
Every human's record is fastened to him and brought out as an open book; it supplies the personal evidence that allows 17:14 to make the human his own accountant.
إِنَّ النَّاسَ قَدْ جَمَعُوا لَكُمْ describes people massed against the believers; faith grows before a threatening gathered force of the kind entered in 100:5.
وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا gives a concrete acquisitive act immediately before the intense love of wealth in 89:20.
أَنَّمَا أَمْوَالُكُمْ وَأَوْلَادُكُمْ فِتْنَةٌ repeats the warning that valued possessions test the human's relation to God.
وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا uses khayr for what the human receives and withholds, a specific character parallel to the possessiveness heard in love of khayr.
لَا يَسْأَمُ الْإِنسَانُ مِن دُعَاءِ الْخَيْرِ joins al-insan to an untiring appetite for khayr; the sense is broader than wealth, but the persistence sharpens the section's diagnosis of attachment.
